Good morning. Today I'm presenting our work on detecting emails and phone numbers for GDPR compliance in cloud food data lakes — a system that's been running in production for eighteen months, and that we validated head-to-head against Microsoft Presidio. The headline result: zero false positives on food data, at the same recall Presidio achieves. Let's walk through why that's hard, how we built it, and how we tested it.

Four parts. First, why this problem is harder than generic PII detection. Second, the detection architecture and how we test it — the methodology is the heart of the paper. Third, the evidence, including a head-to-head comparison with Presidio. And finally, what this means in production and where the limits are.

First, the context: why detecting PII in food data is harder than it sounds.

SOS Food is our own project — a Horizon Europe initiative, January 2024 to December 2027, extending FOODITY into closed-access settings. Both platforms accept CSV uploads from external food-safety providers, up to a gigabyte each, through an asynchronous pipeline. PII detection sits right at ingestion, before the data is ever indexed. So we're under two-sided pressure: false positives cost providers a wasted, abandoned upload; false negatives create GDPR liability the moment the file is searchable. That tension is the whole reason this system exists.

Generic PII tools optimize for broad recall across every PII category. Applied to food data — rich in GPS coordinates, barcodes, nutritional decimals — they flag numeric patterns as phone numbers because their pipeline goes straight from extraction to validation, with no domain-aware filtering step in between. Even though Presidio supports custom recognizers, there's no extension point to inject exclusion rules before its internal detectors run. That architectural gap is what shaped our four design requirements: zero false positives, reliable detection within scope, graceful warnings for ambiguous cases, and streaming so we can handle gigabyte files one line at a time.

So how do we close that gap? A three-layer pipeline that filters before it validates, and a testing methodology that keeps it honest.

Each line of the CSV goes through three layers. Layer one does hard detection: an email regex produces an immediate block, and a permissive regex pulls out phone candidates. Layer two is the key architectural move: eight exclusion patterns eliminate food-data false positives BEFORE the surviving candidates reach phone validation, restricted to European regions via Google's libphonenumber. Layer three is a soft keyword layer that warns without blocking when the hard detector can't confirm PII. This formal per-line decision function D is the contract every test in the suite checks against — and that ordering, filter before validate, is exactly what Presidio cannot structurally do.

Every one of these eight patterns came from an actual production false-positive incident, observed over eighteen months across fifteen pilot organizations — and each one is locked in as a regression test, so a future change can't silently reopen it. This table is essentially our institutional memory of what food data looks like when it isn't PII.

This is the methodological heart of the paper. The difficulty: a detector that reads arbitrary CSV lines has no complete list of right answers — the oracle problem. Metamorphic testing sidesteps it. Start from a seed whose verdict we trust, transform it in a way that must not change the verdict, and check. Here, a phone number reformatted with dots must still be blocked. Our seeds are two-sided: 26 positive ones that must be blocked, which protect recall, and 52 negative ones that must pass, which protect precision. Four relations turn the 78 seeds into 207 generated tests. The same 78 seeds also feed the 500-sample evaluation corpus: the generators enumerate the exclusion families across their parameter ranges and the format and case variants, and 28 samples extracted from real uploads are added (472 synthetic + 28 production-derived). Note that 207 is not a target: it is simply what the generators emit — MR3 alone gives 66 pairs. Adding one seed grows the suite automatically, with no new test code.

Two relations about context. MR1 is the recall side: hide a real email or phone among ordinary food-data fields — here three fields drawn from the negative seeds — and the detector must still block it. MR3 is the precision side, and it is where production incidents come from: individually harmless food values can create a phone-like digit sequence when they end up next to each other in a row. So we combine every pair of our twelve production-derived rows, sixty-six pairs, and each must still pass. The examples on the slide are illustrative.

Two relations about format. MR2: the same phone number written with spaces, dots, hyphens, the double-zero prefix instead of plus, parentheses, or fully compact — six variants per phone seed — must always be blocked. Real providers format numbers every possible way, so this is exactly the kind of bug that slips through hand-written tests. MR4 is the email counterpart: four case variants per email seed — lower, upper, mixed, and domain-only upper. All variants must keep the same verdict as the seed. Again, the examples are illustrative; the exact variants are in the repository.

Now, does it actually work — and how does it compare to the state of the art?

The evaluation corpus has 500 samples in total: 472 synthetic and 28 derived from real production uploads — 300 negatives and 200 positives. Zero false positives across all 300 food-data patterns, including twelve production-derived multi-field CSV rows — that bounds our false-positive rate at 1.3% at the 95% upper confidence bound, with observed precision of exactly 1.000. The sixty misses are almost all deliberately out of scope — non-EU phones, local-format numbers, names, addresses, national IDs — plus exactly one in-scope miss: a French mobile number that libphonenumber itself classifies as VOIP. In-scope recall lands at 99.3%.

We ran Presidio version 2.2.362 on our exact 500-sample corpus, no custom recognizers, no deny-lists — a fair, out-of-the-box comparison. Recall is identical, 0.993; both tools miss the same VOIP-classified number because they share libphonenumber. The difference is precision: all 28 of Presidio's false positives are food values it labels as phone numbers with a score of 0.4 — GPS tuples, customs codes, hyphenated identifiers. Since both systems processed the same 300 negatives, we used McNemar's paired exact test rather than Fisher's: 28 cases where Presidio is wrong and we are right, zero the other way, gives a p-value around seven-point-five times ten to the minus nine. Honest caveat: the 28 errors cluster in three pattern families, so the p-value is an upper bound — but family-level failures cannot be removed by threshold tuning.

It's not enough to have tests that pass — do they actually catch bugs? We ran PIT with default mutators on the detection service: of 73 seeded mutants, 57 were killed, a 78% mutation score. Restricted to just the 207 metamorphic tests, the suite alone kills 60% — so most of the fault-detection power comes directly from the relations. And the process was self-reinforcing: running mutation testing surfaced the gaps that led us to add the boundary and validation unit tests that pushed the full suite from 60% up to 78%.

We sit at the intersection of four lines of work. Generic PII tools give us the baseline and the precision gap we quantify. Schelter's data-quality unit tests are the closest methodological relative — we extend that idea with formalized metamorphic relations. Chen's metamorphic testing framework is what we apply, here, to an oracle-less PII detection problem. Runtime verification frames how to think about our detector: a lightweight heuristic monitor, not a full specification checker. And Gruschka's GDPR-in-big-data analysis is the problem statement we turn into a concrete, testable, deployed answer.

One honest caveat, since this is a testing venue: our corpus isn't independent and identically distributed. Positives are format and case variants of just 26 seeds; negatives instantiate eight exclusion families from 52 seeds. So these confidence intervals bound performance over those families, not an arbitrary provider's upload. What substantiates the bound anyway is the field evidence — 28 samples pulled directly from real production traffic, and eighteen months in production without a single false-positive incident.

To sum up: the contribution here isn't a new detection algorithm — it's standard regexes and a phone validator, made provably precise by a testing methodology. Filtering before validation closes a gap generic tools structurally cannot close. It's been running in production for eighteen months across two platforms with sustained perfect precision. What's next is extending coverage to names and addresses, which will need ML-based NER, plus growing the corpus and formally evaluating that keyword warning layer.

Thank you — happy to take questions. The annotated corpus, the full JUnit 5 suite, and the detection service source code are all in the supplementary repository if you'd like to dig into the details.
